t: A Strange Kind of Glory: Sir Matt Busby and Manchester United
adds: The best single account of how Busby built the club after the war, the Babes and Munich, and the long road to 1968 — written with a journalist's scepticism rather than a fan's.
where: Aurum / Penguin; widely available second-hand and as an ebook

t: Sir Matt Busby: The Definitive Biography
adds: The fuller, later life: Busby's Scottish mining roots, the Manchester City and Liverpool years, and a clear-eyed view of the decline after 1968.

t: The Man Who Kept the Red Flag Flying: Jimmy Murphy
adds: The assistant who missed the Munich flight because of a Wales match and held the club together afterwards; the book that puts Murphy where he belongs.

t: The Lost Babes: Manchester United and the Forgotten Victims of Munich
adds: Munich from the families' side: what the club did and didn't do for the bereaved and the survivors. Uncomfortable and necessary.
The one player every Busby Babe said was the best of them, dead at 21. Reconstructs the career from match reports and the people who saw him.
Charlton on Munich, Busby and Best from the inside; restrained, which is the point.
Law's own account of the Trinity years and the back-heel for City that he still says didn't relegate United.

t: Immortal: The Approved Biography of George Best
adds: The serious Best book — the football first, the decline without the tabloid relish.

by: BBC drama, dir. James Strong — David Tennant as Jimmy Murphy
adds: Ninety minutes on the Babes, Munich and the rebuilt team, told through Murphy and Charlton. The best screen telling of 1958.
where: BBC; DVD and digital rental — availability by region varies

adds: Archive and interviews across the whole arc, from the 1945 appointment to the 1968 final; good on how unusual Busby's authority was for a manager of his time.

by: Documentary, dir. Daniel Gordon (BBC / ESPN 30 for 30)
adds: Best's own voice from the archive against the people who tried to help him. The 1968 footage alone is worth it.
where: BBC; ESPN+ in the US; DVD

t: We're the Famous Man United: Old Trafford in the 80s
adds: The decade before it all worked: Atkinson's cup teams, the terraces, the early Ferguson years, told by the players and the fans who were there.
Captain Marvel on carrying the side through the 80s and handing over to the Ferguson generation.
The youngest World Cup player, the 1985 final winner, and a career over at 26 — frank about what the drinking culture did.

t: Fergie Rises: How Britain's Greatest Football Manager Was Made at Aberdeen
adds: Where the methods came from. Everything he did at United he had already done at Pittodrie, including beating Real Madrid.
The first autobiography, written straight after the Treble with McIlvanney — the better of the two for the Govan years, Aberdeen and the building of the first United side.
The second volume, from the Treble to retirement: Keane, Beckham, Rooney, the Glazers, and how he thought about ending careers. Score-settling in places, which is also useful.
Ferguson as a management text — delegation, discipline, data, succession. Less football, more about how he ran the place.

t: This Is the One: Sir Alex Ferguson, the Uncut Story of a Football Genius
adds: Two seasons of press conferences, 2005–07, by the Guardian's man in the room — the moods, the bans, the comebacks. The closest you'll get to being there.

t: United We Stood: The Unofficial History of the Ferguson Years
adds: A fan's history of the first eight Ferguson years, written as the first title landed; funny and partisan.

t: Glory Glory!: Man Utd in the '90s — The Players' Stories
adds: Interviews with the men who made the 90s, from Pallister and Ince to Kanchelskis and May. The dressing-room version of the decade.

t: Cantona: The Rebel Who Would Be King
adds: A French writer on why Cantona was already a scandal in France and why United was the only place he could have worked. The best player biography on the shelf.

t: The Promised Land: Manchester United's Historic Treble
adds: 1998–99 match by match, with the tactics and the squad politics; the companion to the 99 documentary.
The one with the Haaland tackle and the prawn sandwiches; Dunphy's voice makes it the angriest and most quotable football book of its time.
Saipan, the exit from United, Sunderland and Ipswich — Doyle writes it almost as a monologue, and it reads better than the first.
How the Class of 92 was coached and what it was like to be the one who stayed; good on Ferguson's methods from the players' side.
Short and unshowy, like him. Worth it for what he says about Keane and about tackling.
The goalkeeper of the first great side on Denmark 92, the Treble and why he left a year early.
The quiet midfielder on the 2008 side and on depression after the Moscow final — unusually honest for a player book.
From a Paris suburb to Monaco and the 2008 side; the dressing-room stories are the point.

t: The Anatomy of Manchester United: A History in Ten Matches
adds: The whole history through ten games, with Wilson's tactical reading of each — how United played, not only who won.
The single-volume history from Newton Heath to Ronaldo; the right first book if you want the whole story in order.
Beckham, Giggs, Scholes, Butt and the Nevilles on coming through together, with the 1999 final as the spine.

t: Sir Alex Ferguson: Never Give In
adds: Made by his son after the 2018 brain haemorrhage; Ferguson narrating his own life while recovering his memory of it. Govan and Aberdeen get their due.
The Treble season with nearly every player and Ferguson on camera; Keane on Turin and Schmeichel on the Camp Nou are the highlights.

by: Documentary, dir. Mat Hodgson, narrated by Eric Cantona
adds: Cantona telling the club's story from Busby to Ferguson — a mood piece more than a history, but a good one.

t: Keane and Vieira: Best of Enemies
adds: The two captains, together, going through the tunnel at Highbury and the rest of it. An hour.
where: ITV; clips on the official channels

adds: A Manchester postman is visited by an imaginary Cantona. Not a football film, and the best film with United in it.
where: DVD/digital rental; streaming varies by region

adds: Rooney on Everton, Ferguson, the 2008 side and his own temper, with Coleen alongside; more candid than the autobiographies.
The free school meals campaign — the one time in the post-Ferguson years a United player led the national conversation.

t: The Athletic: Talk of the Devils
by: Podcast — Andy Mitten, Laurie Whitwell and Carl Anka
adds: The best-informed weekly United podcast: reporters who are in the building, with Mitten's long memory of the club. Start with the post-match episodes after a big result.

by: Podcast — Gary Neville, Roy Keane, Jamie Carragher, Ian Wright, Jill Scott
adds: Keane and Neville on United every week, usually disagreeing. The episodes after derbies and after managerial changes are the ones to find.
where: YouTube (The Overlap) and all podcast apps

adds: Long sit-downs with Ferguson, Keane, Scholes, Giggs and the rest of the 90s side — the Ferguson episode is the fullest interview he has given since retiring.

by: Podcast of the fanzine, Andy Mitten
adds: The fanzine's view since 1989, now as a podcast — Old Trafford as the match-going support sees it, away days included.
Fan media at its best when it does the away days and the pre-match atmosphere; see the Links page for the live feed.
